extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (search/classification) and staff using foreign patent documents as prior art
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for USPTO examiners on locating, interpreting, citing, and using foreign patent documents as references (including date verification, INID bibliographic data, country-specific conventions, ordering/copying, and translations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of foreign patents/specifications as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign patents or specifications that were published or issued may be available as references under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) and 102(b); a foreign patent or published specification that claims the priority of a U.S. application (or of an application in another country) may supply an earlier printed publication date or earlier effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether a foreign document claims priority to a U.S. or other earlier application; if so, the earlier application/patent/publication may make the foreign document effective earlier. Example: a British specification claiming priority to a Belgian application may have an earlier effective date because Belgian patents issue soon after filing. Also note countries that publish applications 18 months after filing — such publications may provide an 18-month printed-publication date useful as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check foreign patent family members for earlier publications
rubrics_metrics.description: When a foreign patent family member is located, determine whether any related family member was published or issued at an earlier date that could be used as the reference date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related family members are often printed at different stages (e.g., published application then issued patent). The top-listed document within a related group in the table is the one 'published' first. Examiners must verify that the earlier related document contains the subject matter necessary for the rejection because disclosures are usually identical but can sometimes differ in claims or minor specification details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external patent-document databases and abstracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources not maintained by the USPTO (e.g., Derwent World Patents Index (DWPI), INPADOC, Chemical Abstracts) can be used to locate corresponding patents and earlier publication information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chemical Abstracts publishes abstracts of patents from many countries, abstracting only one family member in full and cross-referencing related family members. Chemical Abstracts is available via commercial databases or on CD-ROM in STIC; examiners should contact STIC to obtain access. Use DWPI/INPADOC to identify family members and publication dates when Office files lack the needed information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of dates shown on face of foreign patent documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner is not required to prove the dates or specifications of foreign patents or applications that the Office has in its possession; certified Office copies constitute prima facie evidence under 28 U.S.C. 1745.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In court, certified copies of the Office copies of these documents are prima facie evidence. An applicant may rebut by competent evidence. The date of receipt shown on Office records or stamped on the copies need only be stated by the examiner when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: When citation dates on face may not be the earliest effective date
rubrics_metrics.description: The citation dates listed on the table or on the face of a foreign document are not necessarily the oldest possible effective dates; earlier effective dates sometimes exist but may not be apparent from the document itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an earlier date is important to a rejection, the examiner should consult STIC staff, who will attempt to obtain further information regarding the earliest possible effective date. STIC can also assist with documents not covered by the table or older documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to use the country/document table (row/box interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each horizontal row of the table contains information on one or more distinct patent documents from a specified country available as references; if several distinct patent documents appear within a common box, they are related documents published at different stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within each box of the second column, the top listed document is the one published first (made available to the public). Once the country/organization and document name are determined, the examiner can see whether a related earlier document with an earlier date is available. Always verify that the earlier related document includes the subject matter necessary for the rejection. Separate rows are provided when a country issues more than one patent type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow country-specific publication and dating conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different patent offices use different document names, date types, and date formats; examiners must be aware of these country-specific conventions when deciding which date to cite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the table: EP (European) prints applications 18 months after priority and EP dates are day/month/year; FR (France) 'date of laying open the application' usually occurs 18 months after filing/priority and is earliest possible date; DE (Germany) may print patents up to four different times and uses a separate DD numbering for first printing; JP (Japan) uses emperor-year notation on older docs (convert by adding 1925 or 1988 as applicable) and INID codes (41)-(47) include emperor-year info. Use the 'GENERAL COMMENTS' and 'FOREIGN LANGUAGE NAME DESIGNATING THE DATE' columns to choose which date is used for citation purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: INID codes: purpose and use for bibliographic data
rubrics_metrics.description: INID (Internationally agreed Numbers for Identification of (bibliographic) Data) codes provide a language-independent means to identify bibliographic data on the first page of patent documents and are used to indicate which bibliographic elements are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INID codes are based on WIPO Standard ST.9 and are used by most patent offices; they were applied to U.S. patents since Aug. 4, 1970. INID codes for industrial designs are similar but not identical and are provided separately. When indicating languages or countries with INID elements, use two-letter language codes per ISO 639:1988 and two-letter country codes per WIPO ST.3 as noted in the guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum and commonly used INID elements for patents (selected list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific INID codes identify bibliographic elements for patents (e.g., identification, number, document kind, filing dates, priority data, publication/making-available dates, classification, title, abstract, references, parties, and PCT/SPC related data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selected codes and uses from the manual (based on WIPO ST.9): (10) identification of the patent document; (11) number; (12) plain language designation of kind of document; (13) kind of document code (ST.16); (15) patent correction information; (19) WIPO ST.3 code identifying the office; (20) data concerning the application; (21)-(23) application numbers and filing dates; (24) date from which rights have effect; (25)-(26) original and published language codes; (30)-(34) priority data and country/office codes; (40)-(48) dates of making available to the public (various forms such as viewing, printing, grant, corrected docs); (50)-(58) technical information including IPC, national classification, title (54), list of prior art (56), abstract/claim (57), field of search (58); (60)-(68) references to related domestic/procedural documents (continuations, reissues, substitutions, etc.); (70)-(76) identification of parties (applicant, inventor, grantee, agent); (80)-(97) PCT/SPC/other convention related data such as designated states, PCT filing/publication data, SPC expiry (94), SPC product name (95), etc. Notes in the manual provide usage specifics (e.g., (41)-(47) are minimum for patent documents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation rules and notes for INID and PCT/priority data
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific presentation rules govern how INID-coded data (especially priority and PCT/regional application data) should be displayed and grouped in patent documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When data coded (31),(32),(33) are presented together, category (30) can be used. For PCT/regional filings, use WO for international applications. Codes (86),(87),(96),(97) (PCT/regional filing/publication data) should be presented together, preferably on a single line, and the application/publication number should contain the republicating office code, document number, and kind code. When multiple applications are referenced, present each set clearly distinguishable (single line or grouped with blank lines). Languages must be indicated using two-letter ISO 639:1988 symbols and countries using WIPO ST.3 two-letter codes. Appendix and notes explain term-of-protection related presentation (e.g., SPC codes).

rubrics_metrics.name: INID codes for industrial designs (overview and required elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: INID codes for industrial designs (based on WIPO ST.80) identify registration/renewal data, application data, exhibition priority, publication dates, reproductions of the design, lists of prior art, characteristic features, and identification of parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selected design INID elements: (10) data concerning registration/renewal; (11) serial number; (12) plain language designation of kind of published document; (14) renewal serial number; (15) date of registration/renewal; (17)-(18) expected registration/expiration dates; (19) two-letter code identifying the authority; (20)-(24) application serial number, filing date, exhibition priority, effective date; (27)-(29) kind/open/sealed, number of designs in application, form of filing; (30)-(33) priority under Paris Convention; (40),(43)-(45) publication dates pre/post examination/registration; (50)-(58) miscellaneous info such as Locarno classification (51), reproductions (55), list of prior art (56), description of characteristic features (57); (60),(62),(66) references to related applications/variants; (70)-(78) parties (applicant, creator, owner, representative, new owner); (80)-(88) international deposit/owner nationality/residence data for Hague Agreement cases. Notes include minimum data elements for design documents and instruction to use two-letter country codes for certain elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining copies and where to find foreign patents in Office systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of foreign patents and published specifications are available via USPTO automated search systems or from STIC; examiners can order copies or make copies themselves and may place copies or translations in the class ‘shoes’ for their art unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent foreign patents are accessible through EAST, WEST, and FPAS and from the Foreign Patent and Scientific Literature Branch (STIC). Older documents are on microfilm or print copies in STIC. Examiners may place a photocopy or translation in the shoes of the class they examine if particularly relevant (see MPEP § 903.03). For documents not in the examiner search files, STIC will obtain copies from its collection or from the originating patent office upon request. For unprinted patent documents, STIC will request that the date of granting and the date made available to the public be indicated on copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of translations and Translation Branch services
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may consult translators in the Translations Branch of STIC for oral assistance and may request written translations of pertinent portions of foreign references being considered or already cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners can get oral translation assistance or request written translations of portions of foreign patents or literature. See MPEP § 901.06(a) (STIC Services - Translations) and MPEP § 903.03 for availability of foreign patents and translation services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date formats and month-name/abbreviation lists for foreign languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign patent publications may present dates using Roman/Arabic numerals in various sequences (day/month/year or year/month/day), and some languages use unique month names that must be translated/mapped to English months for correct citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roman numerals in dates always refer to the month. Japanese publications may show dates in the year of the Emperor; convert by adding 1925 for years prior to 1989 and 1988 for years after 1988 (e.g., 40.3.6 = March 6, 1965). The manual includes alphabetical lists of selected foreign-language month names with their English equivalents and lists of foreign-language names/abbreviations for the United States to help identify whether a foreign-language patent indicates filing in the U.S.
